title: Comparative and superlative

objectives.can: Recognise comparative and superlative forms and read the two ways Greek says 'than'.

explanation.summary: An adjective can say that something is 'stronger', 'greater' or 'least'. Greek makes these comparative and superlative forms by endings or, for a few common adjectives, by a different stem. The thing compared with is then put either in the genitive or after the word ἤ, 'than'.

sections.heading: Three degrees
body: The positive degree is the plain adjective: ἰσχυρός, 'strong'. The comparative says 'stronger' or 'rather strong': ἰσχυρότερος. The superlative says 'strongest', or sometimes just 'very strong': ἐλάχιστος, 'least'.

There are two regular ways to make a comparative. The most common adds -τερος to the stem and then declines like ἀγαθός: ἰσχυρότερος, μικρότερος, πρεσβύτερος. The other has the third-declension endings of ἄφρων (-ων, -ον, genitive -ονος) and is used for some of the commonest adjectives: μείζων 'greater' from μέγας, πλείων 'more' from πολύς, κρείττων 'better', χείρων 'worse', ἐλάσσων 'less'. Superlatives usually end in -τατος or -ιστος and decline like ἀγαθός: ἐλάχιστος, μέγιστος, ὕψιστος, κράτιστος.

sections.heading: How the analysed texts file these forms
body: The analysis used in the library has no feature for degree, and it lists most comparatives under the headword of the positive adjective: μείζων under μέγας, πλείων under πολύς, ἰσχυρότερος under ἰσχυρός, μικρότερος under μικρός. The comparatives κρείττων, χείρων and ἐλάσσων, and the superlatives ἐλάχιστος, ὕψιστος and κράτιστος, are listed as headwords of their own. Whichever way a dictionary or a text lists them, you should recognise the degree from the form and the sense.
Two adjectives you know already are superlative in form but are used as ordinary words: πρῶτος 'first' and ἔσχατος 'last'.

sections.heading: Saying 'than': the genitive and ἤ
body: The first way is to put the thing compared with in the genitive, called the genitive of comparison: ὁ πατὴρ μείζων μού ἐστιν, 'the Father is greater than I'. The second way is to use the conjunction ἤ, 'than', which joins two things in the same case: in πλείονας μαθητὰς ποιεῖ … ἢ Ἰωάννης, Jesus and John are both subjects, so both are nominative. Both ways occur in the New Testament, and the genitive of comparison is very common.
A third, less common way is a preposition: παρά with the accusative, as in διαφορώτερον παρ' αὐτούς, 'more excellent than they'. The sense is the same.

sections.heading: In Koine the comparative often does the work of the superlative
body: A comparative is often used where English would use a superlative: ὁ μικρότερος ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν means 'the least among all of you', and μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη is naturally read 'the greatest of these is love'. The reverse also happens: a superlative form can mean 'very': κράτιστε Θεόφιλε is a courteous title, 'most excellent Theophilus'.

A true superlative with a genitive is read as 'of': ὁ ἐλάχιστος τῶν ἀποστόλων is 'the least of the apostles', where the genitive names the group and does not mean 'than'. Compare it with the genitive of comparison: it is the sense of the sentence that shows which is meant.

misunderstandings: A genitive after a comparative does not mean possession. In μείζων μού the genitive means 'than I', not 'my greater'.
A comparative is not always 'more': πρεσβύτερος can mean 'older' as well as 'elder'. Read it with the noun it belongs to.
μείζων is not a different word from μέγας: it is the comparative of the same adjective, with the third-declension ending -ων as in ἄφρων. Its genitive is μείζονος.

deeper.heading: πρῶτος with a genitive
body: πρῶτος is a superlative in form, but in John 1:15 πρῶτός μου ἦν takes the genitive of comparison, and means 'he was before me'. Grammarians take this as an example of a word that has the form of a superlative and the sense of a comparative. It shows again that the form of a degree word is only a guide to its sense.

examples.analysis: μείζων is nominative singular masculine, the comparative of μέγας, and agrees with πατήρ. μού is the genitive of ἐγώ and means 'than I': a genitive of comparison. The sentence says that one thing is greater than another and does not say how.

examples.analysis: πλείονας is the accusative plural masculine of πλείων, the comparative of πολύς, agreeing with μαθητάς. The second way of saying 'than' is here: ἢ Ἰωάννης, 'than John'. Ἰωάννης is nominative, the same case as the subject Ἰησοῦς that it is compared with.

examples.analysis: κρείττων is nominative singular masculine, with the third-declension ending -ων, and τῶν ἀγγέλων is the genitive of comparison: 'better than the angels'. διαφορώτερον is a comparative in -τερος, and παρ' αὐτούς shows the third way: παρά with the accusative, 'than they'.
